newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Namibian fishing industry in crisis as stocks fall.
newsitem.headline: Namibian fishing industry in crisis as stocks fall.

text.p: The once-vibrant fishing industry of Namibia is facing a crisis with fish stocks at dangerously low levels and industry figures said on Wednesday that it may take many years to recover.
The teeming shoals of pilchards that supported thousands of fishermen in the vast and sparsely populated southern African country have all but disappeared.

Canning company Namibian Sea Products (Namsea), announcing a first-half loss, said on Wednesday that not a single can of locally-fished pilchards had been produced at the canning plants of Walvis Bay this season.
Research scientists said the reason for the collapse was unclear, but that it is most likely a mix of freak natural occurrences and some overfishing.

Stocks have been below normal since 1988, but in 1993 to 1995 a freak body of low-oxygen water entered the Namibian fishing grounds. Though at a depth lower than most fish live, it devastated the food chain and wiped out, or drove away, a generation of young fish before they matured to reproduce.
The fish collapse saw 200,000 Cape fur seals starve to death on the Namibian coast in 1994.
The causes of the phenomenon are unknown. The water could have entered from Angolan waters or be a product of a bloom of local plankton that consumed huge amounts of life-giving oxygen.
"This was a natural event, but for reasons beyond us it has been been much more severe," said one government scientist, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Overfishing has also played a role, including foreign trawlers from countries like Spain.
"We have been fishing these fish at the same time (as the stocks fell). It is not just about the environment," the researcher said.

But industry figures said fishermen kept strictly within quotas designed to keep the stocks viable. "The resource has been managed conservatively for many years. It is not overfishing," said Saul Pick, a director of Namsea and its sister company Namfish.
The one question on everyone minds is can the stocks recover quickly or has long-term damage been done?

The researcher said environmental conditions were now back to normal, but Namibian fish stocks were at a level comparable to that of California in 1954. Those waters have still not fully recovered, he said.

But all agree, just as freak environmental occurrences helped devastate the stocks, they can also revitalise them. "At the moment it is not looking very encouraging, but fishing is a funny game. Tomorrow the fish could be jumping out of the sea," Pick said.
Researchers are less optimistic, but say in a few years stocks could recover. "If we have two or three good years they could come back, but not in just one year," the researcher said.
Other fish stocks too, such as whitefish, are down, but the exact causes are unclear.
Namsea and Namibian Fishing Industries (Namfish) on Wednesday announced they had plunged into the red for the half year to June 30.

Namfish saw attributable income slip to a N$13.63 million ($3.02 million) loss from a N$860,000 ($191,111) profit, while Namsea saw a N$5.05 million ($1.12 million) profit turn into a $N5.31 million ($1.18 million) loss.
The two firms are now deep in merger talks.
